easy.prompt: Which of these is a tautology?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: The law of excluded middle: any proposition is either true or false, so P ∨ ¬P is always true.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Always false (a proposition can't be equivalent to its own negation).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: True only when P is false.

easy.prompt: What does the connective ∧ stand for?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: P ∧ Q is true exactly when both P and Q are true.

easy.prompt: The truth table for P → Q is false in exactly which case?

choices.label: A
choices.body: P is false and Q is true.

choices.label: B
choices.body: P is false and Q is false.

choices.label: C
choices.body: P is true and Q is true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: P is true and Q is false.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Material implication is true except when a true antecedent leads to a false consequent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: True — antecedent and consequent both hold.

easy.prompt: P ↔ Q is true exactly when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: At least one of P or Q is true.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both P and Q are true.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both P and Q are false.

choices.label: D
choices.body: P and Q have the same truth value.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Biconditional is equivalence: both true or both false.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's only half of the biconditional's true cases.

easy.prompt: Which is logically equivalent to ¬(P ∧ Q)?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: De Morgan's law: the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of negations.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the negation of (P ∨ Q), not (P ∧ Q).

easy.prompt: P → Q is logically equivalent to which of the following?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Material implication is true unless P is true and Q is false — same truth table as ¬P ∨ Q.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: False only when both are true — wrong table.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the converse; not equivalent in general.

easy.prompt: An argument is valid if and only if…

choices.label: B
choices.body: It is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Validity is about preservation of truth from premises to conclusion, not about whether premises are actually true.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Valid arguments can have false conclusions when premises are false.

easy.prompt: A sound argument is one that is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Valid and has all true premises.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Soundness requires both validity and actually true premises; this guarantees a true conclusion.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A true conclusion can come from invalid reasoning.

easy.prompt: In first-order logic, ∀x F(x) means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every element of the domain has property F.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exactly one element has property F.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Universal quantification: F(x) holds for all x in the domain.

easy.prompt: ∃x F(x) is logically equivalent to…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Quantifier interchange: 'some F' iff 'not all are non-F'.

easy.prompt: From P → Q and P, we may conclude Q. This rule is called…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: MP is the basic rule for eliminating implications.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MT goes from P → Q and ¬Q to ¬P.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DS uses disjunctions: P ∨ Q and ¬P give Q.

easy.prompt: From P → Q and ¬Q, we may conclude ¬P. This rule is called…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: MT contrapositive reasoning.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: RAA derives a contradiction to refute an assumption.

easy.prompt: How many rows does the truth table of a formula with n distinct atomic propositions have?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Each atomic proposition can be T or F independently.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Underestimates the number of distinct valuations.

easy.prompt: Which formula is a contradiction?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: A proposition can't be true and false simultaneously.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tautology — implication from any P to itself.

easy.prompt: The contrapositive of P → Q is…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original implication.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the negation of the consequent, not contrapositive.

easy.prompt: Affirming the consequent is the invalid pattern:

choices.label: A
choices.body: From P → Q and P, infer Q.

choices.label: D
choices.body: From P → Q and Q, infer P.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Q can be true for many reasons besides P; assuming P is a fallacy.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Denying the antecedent — also invalid, but different from affirming the consequent.

easy.prompt: ¬∃x F(x) is logically equivalent to…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Quantifier negation: 'no F exists' iff 'every x is non-F'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's 'some non-F exists', not 'no F exists'.

easy.prompt: P ∨ Q is false exactly when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both P and Q are false.

choices.label: D
choices.body: P and Q are the same.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Disjunction is inclusive: at least one true makes it true.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The other could still be true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Could be both true or both false.

easy.prompt: A free variable in a formula is one that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Has no value assigned in any model.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Is not bound by a quantifier within the formula.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Free variables stand in for arbitrary objects; sentences (no free variables) are what get truth values.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Models do assign values; free variables are just not bound in the formula.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Multiplicity doesn't matter for being free.

easy.prompt: From P ∨ Q and ¬P, we may conclude Q. This rule is called…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Disjunctive syllogism uses one disjunct's falsity to assert the other.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: MP works on implications, not disjunctions.

medium.prompt: Which of the following is logically equivalent to (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Biconditional is defined as the conjunction of an implication and its converse.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The negation of the biconditional, the opposite.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Doesn't require the truth values to match.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: True only when both are true; biconditional also accepts both false.

medium.prompt: An argument is logically valid iff…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Its conclusion is true in every model where its premises are true.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Its premises are true in every model.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Its conclusion is true in every model.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Validity is semantic preservation: no countermodel where premises hold and conclusion fails.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That makes premises tautologies, also stronger.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That makes the conclusion a tautology — stronger than validity of an argument.

medium.prompt: ∀x ∃y R(x, y) and ∃y ∀x R(x, y) differ in that the second…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cannot be expressed in first-order logic.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Is logically equivalent to the first.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Requires a single y that works for every x.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Order of quantifiers matters: 'some y works for all x' is strictly stronger than 'for every x, some y'.

medium.prompt: Which formula has the same truth table as P ↔ ¬Q?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Both are true exactly when P and Q have different truth values.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Only true when P true and Q false; the biconditional with ¬Q also accepts P false, Q true.

medium.prompt: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) works by…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Assuming P and showing it's true.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Assuming ¬P, deriving a contradiction, and concluding P.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: RAA exploits the law of non-contradiction.

medium.prompt: An interpretation (model) for a first-order language must specify…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only truth values for atomic sentences.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A non-empty domain and an assignment to each predicate, function symbol, and constant.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Truth of a sentence is defined relative to a complete interpretation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ⊥ is logically false in every model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: You also need to interpret the non-logical symbols.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Atomic truth depends on the underlying interpretation.

medium.prompt: Universal instantiation lets you conclude…

choices.label: B
choices.body: F(c) from ∀x F(x), for any term c in the language.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: UI eliminates a universal by picking any term.

medium.prompt: Existential instantiation: from ∃x F(x), you may assume F(c) for a fresh constant c. The 'fresh' restriction is required because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The system uses only finite proofs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Constants must always be fresh in logic.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Otherwise the deduction is too long.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Without it, you could illicitly identify the existential witness with previously-used terms.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: EI introduces a temporary name for an unknown witness; reusing names would over-specify.

medium.prompt: The formula ¬∀x F(x) is logically equivalent to…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Negating a universal yields an existential of the negation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Doesn't account for the outer negation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the negation of an existential, not a universal.

medium.prompt: A countermodel to an argument is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: An interpretation in which all premises are false.

choices.label: B
choices.body: An interpretation in which the conclusion is true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An interpretation in which all premises are true and the conclusion is false.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: A single countermodel suffices to show invalidity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Conclusion truth doesn't matter for invalidity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Models of the conclusion alone tell us nothing about validity.

medium.prompt: Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) expresses a formula as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A disjunction of conjunctions of literals.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A conjunction of disjunctions of literals.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: CNF is the canonical form for SAT solvers and resolution.

medium.prompt: ¬(P → Q) is logically equivalent to…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: P → Q is false iff P is true and Q is false; that's exactly P ∧ ¬Q.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: True only when both are false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's P → Q itself, not its negation.

medium.prompt: In ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)), the variable x is…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bound by ∀x throughout the entire scope.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: x appears under the scope of ∀x, so it's bound.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: It would be free outside the quantifier's scope.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inside this formula, x is bound.

medium.prompt: From P, infer P ∨ Q for any Q. This rule is…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Adding a disjunct to a known truth preserves truth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That uses a disjunction to derive something else.

medium.prompt: Conditional proof / →-introduction lets you derive P → Q by…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Assuming P in a subproof and deriving Q, then discharging the assumption.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Standard deduction theorem rule: assume the antecedent, prove the consequent, conclude the implication.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Q being a tautology gives → trivially, but isn't the general rule.

medium.prompt: Universal generalization allows you to conclude ∀x F(x) from F(c) provided…

choices.label: A
choices.body: c is a specific constant in the language.

choices.label: B
choices.body: c is arbitrary — it does not appear in the assumptions or in F(x).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The constant must not be 'tainted' by other commitments; this guarantees the proof works for any object.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Specific constants can't be generalized this freely.

medium.prompt: A logical consequence relation ⊨ is defined so that Γ ⊨ φ iff…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Γ and φ have the same truth value.

choices.label: B
choices.body: φ is provable from Γ in some proof system.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every model that makes all of Γ true also makes φ true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Some model makes all of Γ true and φ true.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Semantic entailment is preservation of truth across all models.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's syntactic consequence (⊢); they coincide by soundness/completeness.

medium.prompt: Hypothetical syllogism is the rule…

choices.label: A
choices.body: From P → Q and Q → R, infer P → R.

choices.label: B
choices.body: From P ∨ Q and ¬P, infer Q.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Chaining implications.

medium.prompt: First-order logic is undecidable in the following sense:

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every valid formula is also satisfiable.

choices.label: C
choices.body: There is no algorithm that, given any formula, decides whether it is valid.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Church and Turing's undecidability theorem: validity in FOL is recursively enumerable but not decidable.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: True but not what undecidability means.

medium.prompt: A proof system is sound if…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every derivable formula is logically valid.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It contains all axioms of arithmetic.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Soundness ⊢ ⇒ ⊨: provability respects truth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Soundness is a logic property, not arithmetic.

hard.prompt: Gödel's completeness theorem (for first-order logic) says…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every logically valid formula is provable in standard proof systems.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every theorem of arithmetic is true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every true formula has a finite proof.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Together with soundness, completeness gives ⊨ ⇔ ⊢ for FOL.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only formulas valid in all models do.

hard.prompt: Compactness theorem: a set Γ of first-order formulas is satisfiable iff…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every finite subset of Γ is satisfiable.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Compactness has rich consequences: existence of non-standard models of arithmetic, Löwenheim–Skolem applications, etc.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tautologies are trivially satisfiable but don't characterize compactness.

hard.prompt: Löwenheim–Skolem (downward) says that every satisfiable first-order theory in a countable language has…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Downward LS guarantees a countable model, even for theories aiming at uncountable structures (Skolem's paradox).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: First-order theories can have infinite models.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: First-order theories with infinite models have many models of each cardinality.

hard.prompt: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem applies to…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Any consistent, recursively axiomatized theory strong enough to express elementary arithmetic.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Incompleteness needs enough arithmetic for self-reference; weaker systems (e.g., presburger arithmetic) are complete.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Propositional logic is complete and decidable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Some theories are complete (e.g., the theory of real closed fields).

hard.prompt: Resolution is a refutation-complete proof method for…

choices.label: B
choices.body: First-order logic restricted to clausal (CNF) form.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Resolution proves Γ ⊨ φ by deriving the empty clause from Γ ∪ {¬φ} in CNF.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Modal logics need different proof systems.

hard.prompt: An n-ary relation R on a domain D is interpreted in a model as…

choices.label: B
choices.body: A function from D to D.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Relations correspond to sets of tuples.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Formulas are syntax; relations are semantics.

hard.prompt: The propositional SAT problem is NP-complete. Which transformation is canonical for the reduction?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reducing 3-coloring to SAT via Kempe chains.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Cook's reduction: encoding any nondeterministic Turing machine's accepting computation as a CNF formula.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Cook's theorem (1971) showed SAT is NP-complete via direct simulation of NDTMs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's a reduction from 3-coloring, but Cook–Levin is the seminal NP-completeness proof.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That places SAT in PSPACE, but doesn't show NP-completeness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P-completeness is for log-space reductions, not NP.

hard.prompt: Two formulas φ and ψ are logically equivalent iff…

choices.label: A
choices.body: They have the same truth value in every model.

choices.label: C
choices.body: They have the same number of connectives.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Equivalence is mutual entailment: φ ⊨ ψ and ψ ⊨ φ.

hard.prompt: Skolemization eliminates existential quantifiers by…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Replacing existentially-quantified variables with fresh function symbols of the surrounding universal variables.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Replacing them with new constants only, regardless of context.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: If ∀x ∃y R(x, y), Skolemize to ∀x R(x, f(x)) where f is a new function.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Constants only suffice when no enclosing ∀; in general you need functions.

hard.prompt: In modal logic, □P is read as 'necessarily P'. In Kripke semantics, □P holds at world w iff…

choices.label: A
choices.body: P holds at every world accessible from w.

choices.label: C
choices.body: P holds at some world accessible from w.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: The accessibility relation R determines which worlds are 'reachable'; □ is universal over them.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tautologies are necessary in every system, but □P generally isn't a tautology.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Modal operators look beyond the current world.

hard.prompt: Łoś's theorem about ultraproducts implies which classical result?

choices.label: D
choices.body: The compactness theorem of first-order logic.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Łoś's theorem gives a slick model-theoretic proof of compactness via ultraproducts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Tarski's work is foundational but separate.

hard.prompt: Sequent calculus's cut rule is admissible in classical logic, which means…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Any proof using cut can be transformed into a cut-free proof.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Cut cannot be applied at all.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Gentzen's Hauptsatz: cut elimination yields the subformula property, useful for proof analysis.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Cut is a legal rule; it's just removable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cut elimination is a structural result.

hard.prompt: A first-order theory is consistent iff…

choices.label: A
choices.body: It has at least one model.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It contains the law of excluded middle.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Gödel's completeness theorem: consistency (syntactic) ⇔ satisfiability (semantic).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Classical theories typically do, but consistency is independent.

hard.prompt: Robinson Arithmetic Q is weaker than Peano Arithmetic in that…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Q is finitely axiomatized and still allows Gödel's incompleteness theorem to apply.

hard.prompt: Natural deduction's reductio rule lets you conclude ¬P from a subproof in which P leads to ⊥. This rule is…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: ¬I packages a contradiction-from-assumption into a negation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's how ¬ is used, not introduced.

hard.prompt: Two formulas φ, ψ are interderivable iff…

choices.label: B
choices.body: φ ⊢ ψ and ψ ⊢ φ in the chosen proof system.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Interderivability is the syntactic counterpart of equivalence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Both being tautologies makes them equivalent vacuously, but interderivability is stronger relational notion.

hard.prompt: Tarski's truth definition for first-order logic is recursive on…

choices.label: D
choices.body: The structure of formulas, using variable assignments.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: T-schema-style recursion: define satisfaction over atomic, then connectives and quantifiers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Type theory is a different framework.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's Kripke semantics for modal logic.

hard.prompt: Why is propositional logic decidable while first-order logic is not?

choices.label: C
choices.body: Truth in propositional logic can be checked by enumerating 2^n valuations; first-order quantification ranges over potentially infinite domains.

choices.label: D
choices.body: First-order logic has too many connectives.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: The undecidability of FOL is a corollary of Church and Turing's work.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Propositional logic has no predicates or variables.

hard.prompt: If a first-order theory has an infinite model, then by the Löwenheim–Skolem theorems it has…

choices.label: B
choices.body: A model whose cardinality is a prime.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only one infinite model up to isomorphism.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Upward + downward LS together give models of every infinite cardinality ≥ |language|.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Categoricity in all cardinalities is impossible by LS.

hard.prompt: The modal axiom T (□P → P) corresponds to the property of the accessibility relation being…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Sahlqvist correspondence: T ↔ reflexive, 4 ↔ transitive, 5 ↔ Euclidean, B ↔ symmetric.
